opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really different problem. At a place like DeepMind, and especially on something like Gemini, a lot of the recruiting is done for you before you even pick up the phone. The brand is there, the compute is there, and people know that if they join they'll be working on one of the handful of frontier models in the world. You're often choosing among very strong candidates who are already coming to you.

At a small company you don't have any of that by default. Nobody has heard of you, you can't promise thousands of chips, and you usually can't match big-company compensation on cash. So you have to be much clearer about why someone should take the risk. In my experience it comes down to a few things.

First, ownership and scope. On a huge team, even a very senior person might own one slice of the pretraining pipeline or one eval area. At a small company, one person might own the whole data strategy or the entire post-training stack. For a certain kind of person, that's exciting, and those are the people you want.

Second, speed. Large organizations have a lot of coordination cost: reviews, alignment across teams, launch processes. That exists for good reasons, but some researchers and engineers really want to try an idea on Monday and see it in production a week later. You have to show them that's real, not just something you say in the pitch.

Third, the mission and the specific bet. You can't out-general a big lab, so you need a sharp thesis about what you're doing differently. Candidates are very sophisticated now. They'll ask, "Why won't Google or OpenAI just do this?" You need a good answer.

And finally, you have to be selective in a different way. At a big lab, you can hire someone who's excellent at one narrow thing and surround them with support. At a startup, every early hire shapes the culture and has to be comfortable with ambiguity, wear multiple hats, and do the unglamorous work too. So in some ways the bar is higher, even if the pool is smaller. One wrong hire on a team of ten matters much more than on a team of a thousand.

So it's harder, but the conversations are also more honest. You're not selling a logo. You're asking someone to make a bet with you, and the people who say yes for the right reasons tend to be exactly who you want.

r001.rationale: The response says candidates must be persuaded to “take the risk” of joining a small company, contrasting that with DeepMind’s established brand, compute, and frontier-model work.

r002.rationale: It discusses ownership, speed, mission, and a specific thesis as reasons to join, but does not identify the chance to build a company that could become the next OpenAI or Anthropic.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because I've sat on both sides of it. At Gemini, honestly, recruiting is almost a filtering problem rather than a sourcing problem. The brand does the work. People come to you because they want to be near the frontier, they want the compute, they want the name on their resume. Your challenge there is really about picking the right people out of an enormous pool and then making sure they don't get lost in a thousand-person org.

At a small company it's the inverse. You have no gravitational pull on your own. Nobody wakes up thinking, "I want to join this twelve-person startup." You have to go find them, and then you have to convince them, and the conversation is completely different. You can't say "you'll train the biggest model in the world," because you won't. What you can say is, "you'll own a problem end to end, your work will ship in weeks instead of quarters, and you'll actually see whether it mattered."

And what I've found is that this naturally selects for a different kind of person. The people who are drawn to the big lab often want the resources and the stability, and that's a completely legitimate thing to want. The people who come to a small company tend to be more comfortable with ambiguity. They don't need a clearly scoped project handed to them. They're fine saying, "this doesn't exist yet, I'll figure it out." So in a way, the recruiting difficulty is also a filter. If somebody needs to be sold hard on the size and the brand, they probably aren't going to be happy with you anyway.

The hardest part, I think, is not getting the first conversation. It's that you're competing on comp with companies that can pay almost arbitrary amounts, and you really can't win that fight head on. So you have to be honest about what you're offering, which is equity with real upside, a lot of ownership, and the chance to be early on something. Some people hear that and it's exactly what they want. Most people don't, and that's fine. You only need a handful of the right ones.

r001.rationale: The response says small companies lack brand pull and that some candidates prefer the resources and stability of a large lab, but it does not clearly attribute the recruiting difficulty to candidates perceiving greater risk in joining the small company.

r002.rationale: The response mentions equity upside and being early at a company, but does not identify the chance to build the next OpenAI or Anthropic as a motivation.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is what you can offer people. On the Gemini team, you have substantial compute, strong infrastructure, and colleagues with deep expertise across many areas. You can work on models that reach a huge number of people. For a small company, it’s difficult to compete on those same dimensions.

What you can offer is ownership and a much more direct connection between someone’s work and the company’s direction. A researcher or engineer can help decide what to build, run the experiment, and see how it affects the product. That appeals to a different set of motivations.

So recruiting becomes very much about finding people who believe in the particular problem you’re solving and want that level of responsibility. You also have to be honest about the constraints. Some people do their best work with the resources and support of a large team; others are excited by the freedom and uncertainty of building something small.

r001.rationale: The response mentions constraints and uncertainty at a small company, but it does not identify candidates’ perception of greater risk as the reason recruiting is harder.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the motivation of helping build a company that could become the next OpenAI or Anthropic.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is different. On a team like Gemini, you have a lot of resources—compute, infrastructure, and strong researchers around you. You can work on problems at a scale that’s very hard for a small company to match, and that’s a big attraction for candidates.

For a small AI company, you need a clear answer to: why should someone join us? It might be a particular problem they really care about, more ownership, or the ability to move quickly and see their work reach users. One person can have a much bigger influence on the direction of the company.

So I wouldn’t try to compete purely on resources. The challenge is finding people who are excited about what being small makes possible, and being honest with them about the uncertainty and the constraints.

r001.rationale: The response mentions being honest about uncertainty and constraints, but it does not say that candidates perceive greater risk as the reason recruiting is harder for a small AI company.
